message.content:
**Hydrogen – Key Physical & Chemical Properties**

| Property | Value / Description | Notes |
|----------|---------------------|-------|
| **Atomic number** | 1 | Only one proton in the nucleus. |
| **Symbol** | H | From Latin *hydro* “water”. |
| **Standard atomic weight** | 1.008 u | Weighted average of its naturally occurring isotopes. |
| **Isotopes** | Protium (^1H), Deuterium (^2H), Tritium (^3H) | Deuterium and tritium are stable/unstable; used in nuclear fusion research. |
| **Electron configuration** | 1s¹ | One valence electron. |
| **State at STP (0 °C, 1 atm)** | Gas | Extremely low density. |
| **Density (STP)** | 0.08988 g L⁻¹ | About 14 times lighter than air. |
| **Melting point** | –259.16 °C (−434.69 °F) | Solidifies only at cryogenic temperatures. |
| **Boiling point** | –252.87 °C (–423.17 °F) | Vaporizes at very low temperatures. |
| **Heat of vaporization** | 0.449 kJ g⁻¹ | Low latent heat. |
| **Specific heat (gas, 25 °C)** | 14.304 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ | High specific heat relative to its mass. |
| **Viscosity (gas, 25 °C)** | 8.76 × 10⁻⁶ Pa·s | Very low viscosity. |
| **Molar volume (ideal gas, 25 °C)** | 22.414 L mol⁻¹ | Standard molar volume. |
| **Electronegativity (Pauling)** | 2.20 | Highest among all elements. |
| **First ionization energy** | 13.598 eV (1312 kJ mol⁻¹) | Energy required to remove the single valence electron. |
| **Electron affinity** | 72.8 kJ mol⁻¹ | Energy released when gaining an electron. |
| **Bond dissociation energy (H₂)** | 436 kJ mol⁻¹ | Strength of the H–H covalent bond. |
| **Dipole moment (H₂)** | 0 D | Homonuclear diatomic, no permanent dipole. |
| **Reactivity** | Highly reactive, forms hydrides with metals and nonmetals. | Combines with oxygen to form water, reacts with halogens, etc. |
| **Flammability** | Extremely flammable | Burns with a pale blue flame; can form explosive mixtures with air (1–4 % H₂). |
| **Uses** | Fuel (fuel cells, rocket propellant), industrial hydrogenation, ammonia synthesis, metal processing, laboratory reagent. | Widely used in chemistry labs and industry. |

### Quick Takeaways

- **Lightest element** – only one proton and one electron.  
- **Highly reactive** – forms bonds readily, especially with electronegative atoms.  
- **Low boiling/melting points** – exists as a gas under normal conditions.  
- **High electronegativity** – attracts electrons strongly.  
- **Key isotope applications** – deuterium used in heavy water reactors; tritium in nuclear fusion experiments.  

These properties make hydrogen unique among the elements, enabling its use as a clean fuel, a reducing agent, and a building block in many chemical processes.
